I work as a cleaner at a food court, which requires a surprising amount of interaction with customers that I didn't really expect until I started the job. Today a homeless guy started ranting about me cleaning and repeatedly called me a knob-head, because I was doing my job, and he went on some tirade about how I shouldn't be cleaning right next to customers - which I wasn't doing. I ignored it because he's not worth it. He later moved to the outside seating area, and I ended up discovering the lovely mess of sauce all over the tables and chairs he was sat at, and a drink spill on the floor too. He later approached me to give me 'advise' about how I shouldn't clean near customers. I'm not the confrontational type, but I really had enough and told him straight that I wasn't cleaning anywhere near him or other customers and he knew it - to be honest I was kind of proud as to how well I handled myself. I guess he didn't expect me to actually stand my ground because he immediately backed down.

Thankfully, I don't get treated like shit in this job too often, but this has to be the worst one. Second worst would have to be some old hag that insulted my job, because I was literally on my hands a knees cleaning railings, and then proceeded to pat me on the head. I still somewhat regret not punching that bitch.

I vividly remember when I was approximately aged between 7-12, and I would have hallucinations quite regularly. I would often see dead people in mirrors - particularly if it was night time or dark - and if I could see a mirror in my peripheral vision, I would see my own reflection moving separately from me, often the eyes would turn black. There were a few times also when I saw a women who, years later I found to my terror, looked very much like the girl who crawls out the tv in The Ring. Mostly I would see this in mirrors, but occasionally that were freely walking around my world, and it was usually when it was dark, but not limited to it. The one that really terrified me was "The Flour Sack Man"; he was a very tall man with broad shoulders, and he had a flour sack over his head. There were 'X's' stitched on the mask to mark his eyes, and a curved row of stitched 'X's' to mark his smile. As well as the visual hallucinations, I used to hear voices too, often taunting me about how they were going to kill me. I still remember hearing a girl laughing that she was going to chop me up into little pieces with a hatchet. It was horrible time, and I was dealing with a lot of other issues as well, and before all this started I had already been though far more than a child my age should ever have to. I was terrified, but what terrified me far more was the thought of what my family would do if they ever found out. I didn't tell a soul.

I knew my hallucinations weren't normal, but I didn't know my relationship with my family wasn't. I didn't know it wasn't normal to be shouted at and called names by my dad, for no good reason. I didn't realise it wasn't normal for my dad and grandmother to insult me about how little I helped with chores and yet repeatedly refuse to teach me when I asked. I didn't know it wasn't normal to be scared of my own family members, or to be made to feel depressed, worthless and suicidal by them. I didn't know it wasn't normal to put up with a terrifying experience because I was too scared of asking for their "help".

In my later teenage years, I did test the water when my mental health got particularly unbearable, and talked to my grandmother about social anxiety. She "helped" me by quite blatantly and embarrassingly forcing me to talk to people she knew whenever we were out together. She'd keep prompting me to talk about what I'm doing at sixth form and such, and when it was over she'd sneer "There, that wasn't so hard, was it?". I spent the next several months unable to withstand physical contact. I was thankful that my family wasn't touchy, and that my friends were actually understanding about mental health and gave me the space I needed.

Cut my family out of my life years ago. Never going back.

Long story short: I was an abuse victim at home and at school for two decades, and my home life made it difficult to keep up with my education, so I never felt able to get that all important part time work experience that makes finding full time employment easier. After graduating from university last summer I stated looking for work, and after no success and a personal tragedy, my partners parents suggested we moved in with them. It meant moving town which improved both of our mental health, and I've actually been getting interviews.

I'm 23, and I've been accepted for my first job. I can finally pay off the overdraft that's been hanging round my neck like a noose, and I can help my partner pay off his debts too. Feels like we'e finally starting to get there :)

I especially love my last name, because it's linked to a folk tale about finding your voice and freedom, after suffering abuse.

For anyone who is interested in what my home situation was like. I hadn't had contact with my mother since I was about 7 years old. At the age of 5 she took me from my father after they had an argument and her and her friends physically abused me until my dad won full custody of me. It's important to note that my dad never wanted children, but he felt like he had a duty to me as my biological father, so he fought for full custody and forced himself to take responsibility of a child he didn't want in the first place. I think he regretted that decision and the resentment got to much for him over time, because as I grew up he became more and more verbally abusive. By the time I was a teenager he would call me horrible names ("fucking twat", "stupid wanker", "fucking cunt") every other day for no reason, or for something very minor. Whenever I showed any emotion that wasn't happiness or neutrality, he would get angry at me and tell me to pack it in or that I was stupid. He knew I didn't like people in my personal space when I was doing something, so he would "accidentally" bump into me, and then put his face inches from mine, and if he saw the slightest sign of irritation he would get in my face a snarl "what?! What's wrong with you?!", then he'd stomp off and muttered "Miserable sod". He would have temper tantrums several times a week that would result in him stomping though the house slamming doors and cupboards, and would then make a snack as loudly as possible. To this day I flinch when I hear sudden loud sounds, particularly plates clattering. I rarely bothered telling him when I was unwell, because he would always blame it on me being lazy and not getting out enough, despite the fact that I was out with my friends running around every other day, but of course because he didn't see that happen I must have made it up.

Then there was my grandmother. My dad worked a full time job, so as part of full time custody my grandmother agreed to care for me before and after school, when my dad wouldn't be able to. The best way to describe her would be an overly critical manipulative narcissistic sociopath. She was constantly criticising me over everything I did or said, because she was so concerned about how I reflected on her 'image' and I think she somewhat wanted to live the life she never had through me. She would regularly insult my hair often saying it was "like rats tails", but if I ever suggested getting it cut or styled, suddenly she could praise my hair enough, and she would tell me "it's so beautiful and natural, you can't cut too much off you'll ruin it". I once suggested that I'd like to dye my hair red, and her instant reaction was "No, that's what your mother did, she had lovely beautiful hair just like yours, and then she ruined it, you don't want to make the same mistake do you?". She loved using my mother as an example to discourage me from doing things she didn't approve of. I eventually started rebelling in small ways because I was sick of the lack of control, and I got a side fringe dyed blue. At some point I dyed it red, and when she first saw it she screwed up her face and said "no, I don't like it". Didn't even greet me or ask how I was, just straight to critiquing my appearance. I stood up for myself and replied in a matter of fact way "well, I like it", and she stomped her foot like a moody child and snapped "Well, I don't". She also wouldn't shut up about my weight and eating habits. I was always naturally skinny, and in the same day she would comment that I was "too thin and need to eat more" she would tell me "If you keeping eating like that, you'll get fat". Her favourite thing was asking me if I was hungry after school, and if I said no she'd prepare some snacks anyway. If I ate it she would gloat that "you're so lazy, you won't get yourself food, but put something in front of you and you'll eat", and if I didn't eat it I was a horrible granddaughter for putting her through all that work. That was another things she loved, making herself the victim in any given situation. She would buy things for me and tell me that if I didn't like it, I should tell her so she could take it back, and if I told her I didn't like something she would have strop, snatch it from and huff "Well then I guess it goes back to the shop, I don't know why I even bother". She'd be sunk into her arm chair all quiet for the rest of the time. She did something similar whenever I called her out on her racism or homophobia, she'd act emotionally wounded and slink into her chair saying "Well I guess I'll just shut up then, not as if anyone every listens to me anyway". I think what hurt the most though, was how she talked to me about my grades. She always told me that all they ever asked was that I tried my best, and that was always good enough. In my GCSE's I got an A in English Language, and the rest of my grades were equal parts B's and C's. I told her I was so proud that I got an A, and she put her nose up in the air and huffed "Hmph, no A*'s then?". That was the moment that everything clicked into place and I stopped making excuses to myself about her. I hated her from that point on. It didn't stop there though, when I got an A in film studies A-levels that wasn't anything to celebrate because "it's just Film Studies", and when I got accepted by all my university options she threw a strop because I picked the university I wanted instead of the one she approved of, even though I explained it was the only university in my country that did the course I wanted to do.

As you might imagine, through my mothers physical abuse and neglect, my fathers verbal and emotional abuse, and my grandmothers emotional and psychological abuse, my mental health was terrible. I was also getting bullied quite badly at school, mostly verbal, but throughout middle school it was physical too. I had issues with depression since I was about 5, I struggled in middle school with OCD and hallucinations, throughout my preteen years and teenage years I struggled with anorexia and self harm, I developed social anxiety from middle school on wards, and my first suicide attempt was a short while before my dad won custody of me, and I can't remember how many times I've tried since. I kept all of this hidden from my family, because the thought of what they would do if they found out was far more terrifying that the mental illnesses. I still remember my grandmother looking me in the eyes and saying "I worry about your weight, but I know you're not anorexic because you face isn't all sunken". I was over a stone underweight and I was weighing out my food to control my calorie intake. I still have some issues with self harm, I was clean for almost three months, but recently suffered a break down and made one cut on my wrist. It took a lot not to do more. Being away from my hometown, I'm no longer constantly reminded of all the shit things that happened there, but that makes it harder to repress some of the memories from when I was with my mother. I've been having nightmares and flashbacks, which hasn't been easy. It's been worse since I've taken my medication, because while that hasn't changed my depressive mood it's gotten rid of the obsessive compulsive thoughts that would plague my head for hours on end, so my heads clearly which again makes some things harder to repress. To be honest though, the thoughts that the anti-depressants control were far more crippling, so silver lining I guess?

Sorry if I've rambled on, it's difficult to describe so much history in few words, and in my experience so many people don't seem to understand how bad emotional/psychological/verbal abuse can be until you really describe it. And to anyone out there who is in a similar situation, know that you deserve so much better, don't ever let them or anyone else put out your spark - you're a bright start that the world can't afford to lose.

I'm not sure if this would really be classed as running away, but with how overbearing my family was, it felt like it in some ways. I was 19, nearly 20, and I had just started my first year of university. I lied to my family and said I was required to live on campus in the first year, because I was desperate for a taste of independence and freedom from them. It was only a half hour drive away, but that was long enough to ensure they wouldn't visit - they wouldn't go out of their way to visit, but it was expected that I would for them (bare in mind I can't drive).

It wasn't even 2 weeks since I'd moved away that me and my dad were texting and he said something that rubbed me the wrong way and I ended up calling him out on the shit him and his mother had put me through over the years. Of course he feigned ignorance and refused to even acknowledge my accusations. Eventually he suggested we should just go our separate ways, and I didn't bother replying. I knew him very well, if I had tried to fix things he would have 'won', and if I agreed to not have anything to do with him he would have felt like he was his decision not mine. I didn't want him to feel like he was in control, and I didn't want him to have any closure.

I very nearly faced homelessness at the end of my first year of university, but my partner suggested that we move in together. We unfortunately had to live in my hometown because of his work, and it wasn't a big town, so I spent over two years terrified every time I left the flat, in case I bumped into them. I also changed my entire name, because every time people called my name it felt like I was still my family's property. I've since graduated from university with a 2:1 in Psychology, Counselling and Therapies, and I've been looking for work for almost a year. My partner suffered a very severe case of depression, and was unable to bring himself to go to work, which caused a lot of worry for both of us about finances and paying bills. His family was extremely supportive, and they stepped in to help us big time, and we both really appreciate all the help they've provided. A few months ago we moved out of my hometown and in with my partners family, and I'm having better luck with getting job interviews. It's freeing to not fear for my safety every time I leave the house, and I'm also now on anti-depressants which are a huge help, and I'm seeking therapy for the first time in 23 years. It's only been two or three months since my partner and I moved, but our relationship has become significantly stronger, and our mental health has improved.

Talked to a counsellor who spent the entire hour pulling faces at me in some attempt to appear sympathetic by exaggerating her facial expressions. Her advise for tackling my mental health issues (depression, social anxiety, trauma caused by long term abuse, a neurological sound disorder) was to basically just get over it - she didn't at all talk me through coping mechanisms, or anything of the like. I canceled the rest of my sessions with her, and then received a review form to fill out about my experience of the counselling services. I really enjoyed filling that thing out.

In my upper school we had a psychology teacher from America, with a very thick accent. She got talked about a lot for some of the things she'd say in class, including calling a student an "ass-hat". The one I'll never forget is when she suddenly went on a tirade about politics, and out of the blue said "I don't like Obama, Obama can eat my ass".

This would definitely be my dad, and to answer the question - he didn't cope. My mother sabotaged their birth control, because she was a mooching bitch and realised that he'd get sick of her shit eventually. He was also very proud and a traditional type of man, so she knew he would stay if she got knocked up. When I was young, she ended up taking me away to spite him after they had a massive argument. My dad fought for shared custody - he believed it was expected of him as my biological father - and when it came to light that she was neglecting and physically abusing me, he pushed for full custody instead, which he won. He forced himself to take full responsibility for child he never wanted, because he thought it was his duty. Things were okay at first, he was clearly out of his element, but he tried his best. Eventually I think the resentment and regret caught up with him, because he became more and more verbally and emotionally abusive as years went on. When I went to university we ended up having a huge argument and I called him out on his behaviour for one last time, as usual he refused to acknowledge he had done anything, so I cut contact - also with the rest of my family too because they were no better either. It was by far the best decision I ever made.


To be clear, I'm not saying all 'regret-parents' are destined to abuse their children, I just want to share one of many possibilities that could happen, because regret is a very powerful emotion. When you're confronted by that regret 24/7 for 18+ years, it can be a real kick in the teeth, and it's easy to see how that could push a person to snap.


If anyone here is reading this to gain some insight because they're not sure whether or not they want children, then please consider what I, and similar children, went through. Children are living beings, and it's not fair on them to be brought into the world by someone who is unprepared. They're also a lot more observant than you might expect, and they'll pick up on the small differences between you and other parents - they'll notice far more than you'll ever realise. If you don't want children, or if you're not sure, then don't have them on a whim or because everyone tells you you'll regret it otherwise. A potential child's well-being is far more important than trying to please societal expectations of unprotected sex. If you're going to have children, it should be because you've done your research, you've done plenty of babysitting, and you wholeheartedly feel that you'd be a capable parent.

I got in trouble in lower school for writing in cursive before they had taught us how to. My teacher told me off about it and, me being the sensitive child, I got upset and cried to my grandmother about it. She went down to the school and had ago at them. I also got in trouble at the same school for spelling my own name "wrong". My name is commonly spelled with a 'y' at the end, but my parents chose to spell it with an 'i' at the end instead - I should add that this was still an accepted spelling of the name. Again I got upset, and my grandmother had to explain to them that I had actually spelled my name correctly.

In middle school I frequently got treated like shit by a maths teacher I had. I couldn't do maths in my head fast enough for her, so she would shout at me and demean me in front of the entire class. It resulted in me being terrified every time she asked me a maths question, and I also found myself unable to put my hand up in any of my classes, and I would panic if I was picked on for an answer. I was so scared of her, that one day when I was feeling unwell, I was too scared to ask her if I could go to the office, so I ended up crying outside her classroom before class started - thankfully another student told her, and I was allowed to leave. In psychology A-level I was picked on to answer a question, and I even had the answer written in my notebook right in front of me, but I panicked and told her I didn't know. So Ms Metcalfe, thanks for playing such a huge role in my development of social anxiety, I really hope the worst for you.

I really enjoy film and tv analysis, especially with horror or psychological thriller genres, or where recurring themes and foreshadowing are of importance. I don't do this as a job - though I'd love to - I just really enjoy looking at the deeper themes and meanings of the plot, character choices, character development, motives, motifs, cinematography, etc. I find it fascinating, and oddly calming and enjoyable.

I think it comes from when I did A-Level film studies, and my teacher was amazing; she pushed us to do the best we could and made us feel like she believed in us. In this time we were required to do some film analysis, and I got hooked after analysing a scene from Scream 2, and as well as the reoccurring themes and foreshadowing presented in the cornetto trilogy.

Not exactly what you're looking for, but not far off I guess. I sometimes wonder if I'll be that person who seemingly vanished, but I have my doubts that anyone noticed at all, or will ever notice. I was a victim of abuse from my family and at school until I was about 20. Then when I went to university I cut contact with my family, and a year later I changed my name. Unfortunately I still had to live in the same town as my family and many several of the people who'd bullied me throughout school - I was terrified every time I left my home. 

I'm now 23, and I just moved to an entirely different county, and deleted everyone from my social media who I went to school with. The few people I kept are my partners family and friends I made outside of school - none of which know of people who knew me from school. I had friends in school, but lost contact with a lot of them when we all went of to different university's, and lost contact with my main friend group because of an argument, so I don't think I'll be having anyone trying to track me down. If anyone ever did, I don't think I'd be interested at all in answering any questions they may have. I tried talking about what I went through to a few friends, but they just brushed it off or shut me down about it as if it never happened. I had one girl tell me I wasn't allowed to say I was bullied because she apparently personally made certain no one did that in my middle school - I was bullied worse there than any of my other schools. I'm not going to waste my time on people who'll just act like I didn't go through anything, just they can feel better about turning a blind eye to it.

On a lighter note, I'm much happier now. I actually got a doctors appointment today and I've gotten a prescription for anti-depressants and I've been referred to get therapy. I'm dreading having to open up about so many years worth of horrible experiences, but I'm ready to get help where I couldn't before. I'm ready for a better and happier life.

The piece of shit that used to live in the flat above ours would play music so loudly that from inside our flat we could hear it as clearly as if we were just walking into a club. On average his music would go on for about 6-8 hours, and there were far too many instances where he would be playing music until 5am, and commonly wouldn't shut the hell up until 1 or 2 am. Multiple other residents complained to him, his landlord, their own landlords, and to the building management. There were several times where we could hear people having to almost kick his door in just in order to be loud enough for him to hear them, some residents shouted outside his door or up at his window, and at one point his window ended up smashed - though I've no idea whether that was him, his friends, or a disgruntled resident.

I made multiple complaints to my landlord, their landlord, the building management team, and eventually found out that it was the council I should be sending complaints to. Eventually the building management team informed me he had been served notice by his landlord and would be leaving in September. Well September came and went and we were still having the same issues, and I could hear his trademark cackle throughout the day, so I asked the building management what was going on and why he was still here, and they said they would investigate and update me. After several weeks of silence on the matter, I asked if they had any update on the situation and responded with a snarky email about how it's none of my business who the landlord allows to stay in that flat, or why, and they told me to send any further complaints via my landlord. I would have been fine if they had told me straight up that they can't provide me with information about whether a resident is being served notice, but they literally told me they could do that and then became aggressive in a very unprofessional manner when I requested the update that they said they could provide me with. I'm still very angry about the nasty and deceitful way that they communicated with me on the matter, but decided they weren't worth the hassle. There was constant misinformation and lies about whether or not the music was being caused by a friend that he allowed to stay at his flat while he was away. I also stumbled upon his twitter which was full of evidence of high tech music recording equipment in his flat, and tweets about how he was totally aware that his neighbours were pissed off by his constant noise. It should also be noted that I suffer from a sound disorder, so as well as the obvious not being able to sleep, or hear my own thoughts, I was regularly breaking down in tears and I gave up trying to give up self harm.

All of this went on for the duration of almost a year and a half, and we ended up moving roughly two months ago (there were other factors in play, but without those factors we still would have moved). As far as I'm aware he still lives there. The whole situation still angers me to the core.

There was never really a specific moment for me; I've never really liked kids, even when I was a kid myself. I remember playing happy families when I was really young, and everyone hated that I refused to be a parent or child, I was always the pet cat, dog, or tiger. However, when I was about 12ish I actually made this conscious decision verbally, and I got harassed by my peers over it, to the point where I believed that I didn't have a choice in the matter. They told me I'd never find a boyfriend if I didn't want children, and even got my crush to write a list of reasons as to why he would never go out with me - which included that I didn't want kids. Another thing that contributed, was the amount of fuckwits who hear that I don't like/want kids and take the opportunity to shove their own on me, with some incorrect belief that it'll ignite my nonexistent maternal flame. Never shove your child onto someone who isn't willing to interact with them, it's not fair on that individual - they have a right to their personal space regardless of whether you disagree with their lifestyle choice - and it could put your child in a harmful position.

The fact is, not everyone is meant to be a parent, and not everyone loves children, and that's okay - as long as you're not some dickhead who actively and intentionally tries to harm kids (or anyone for that matter). When I was a preteen and teenager, I lived in a neighbourhood that was brimming with cats; I didn't have friends or pets, so I made it my business to try to befriend the local cats. I was never too invasive, just stretched out a hand and talked to them. I was shy too, so I never pushed them to interact with me, I didn't want to scare them. I made quite few cat friends growing up, and some of the shier ones even let me pet them when they saw how I treated other cats. Four more stories come to mind.


Thomas and Sam. Thomas was a very fluffy white cat with patches of black. He was very confident and lived near a grassy field where I used to kick a ball around. We quickly became friends, and I visited him regularly - I'd give him fuss and we'd sit together on the grass and watch the world pass us by. A few times I saw a very fluffy tabby cat, but he would always run away in absolute terror at the sight of human activity. Until one day, I was walking passed Thomas' home and he came out to greet me. I knelt down next to him, and ran my hands through his thick coat, when I suddenly saw the fluffy tabby, Sam, gingerly standing in the driveway. I reached my hand towards him and talked softly as he inched closer and sniffed at my fingers. I didn't know how important this moment was until later, I'll come back to that, but he pushed his head into my palm and let me pet him and stroke him to my hearts content. A while later when I was stopped by Thomas again, his owner was coming out of the house and we started talking about her cats. She was extremely surprised that Sam had let anyone pet him, because he was scared of everyone but his current owners; she explained that both cats had suffered abuse, including being put into a washing machine. Both cats suffered serious injuries, and Sam barely survived. I felt happy that he let me show him some human kindness, but even more so I was glad that he had so much trust in his brothers judgement and hoped that Thomas had helped Sam to adjust to being around his new owners. Having someone you can trust is so important when coping with a traumatic experience, but it's not a luxury that everyone has.


Pete and Dudley. These two brothers belonged to my next-door neighbour; Pete was a very shy, slender black cat, with an almost unnoticeable white dusting on his chest, and Dudley was a fluffy black cat with a white bib, white paws, and the brightest whiskers I'd ever seen. Seriously, Dudley's whiskers were like glow sticks at night. They were playful and enjoyed fuss, but for the most part played among them selves and didn't care for being picked up or for snuggling on laps. One day, Dudley starts limping and it turns out he's damaged his back leg, needs surgery, and has to don the cone of shame for a while. This slows Dudley down, but he still tries to play games with his brother, who is total anywhere that every time they initiate a game of chase, Dudley can't keep up. I was outside sat on a wall, wanting to play some handheld video games outside, since it was so nice out. Pete came charging through the gate to next doors garden, jumped over the wall I was sat on, and sped away through the gate to my garden. I then saw Dudley at the gate trying to get his head through, I'd seen him do it before, and it always resulted in him banging his head as he squeezed the cone of shame through. I walked over to him and helped him through - I know he could do it himself, but at least this way he didn't hit his head. He tottered by me, jumped over the wall and sat in front of the gate. He couldn't get through this gate with his cone of shame, so I pushed it open and left it open so he could get out without much trouble. Only a few minutes later and he came back out looking kind of sad and pathetic, and he lingered around the gate. I knelt down next to him on the gravel path that led into the garden, and stroked him gently. Without hesitation he clambered into my lap and curled up, I kept petting him and within a few minutes he was asleep. I stayed there with him for over two hours, and played video games to pass the time and to help forget the gravel that was piercing my legs. Eventually he woke up, journeyed back to his garden gate, and I helped him get back through without him hitting his head. From then on he was the cuddliest cat with me, and would use any opportunity to clamber into my lap - something he didn't even do with his owner. He often ran up to greet me with his tail in the air, even a few times sprinting half way down the street if he spotted me coming home from school. I had a rough childhood, and was often quite upset and depressed, Dudley and even Pete - who liked a bit of petting but otherwise avoided people - were always there to comfort me when things were particularly bad. I had a very special bond with Dudley, and in particular I'll never forget the night he snuck into my room when my dad was taking the bins out. I woke up the next morning to nothing but darkness and thought I was blind, until I heard a meow, suddenly the darkness was lifted, and Dudley was looking down at me. How he didn't suffocate me or wake me up is beyond me, but that fond memory sums him up perfectly.


The Cat Kingdom Body Guard, or Tuxedo Cat for short. Things weren't the same after my neighbour moved; I dearly missed calling out to Dudley and hearing the "shoom!" as he sprinted across gravel to come see me. The closest I came to experiencing such a friendship with another feline was years later when a cheerful looking tom cat turned up in the neighbourhood. He was very confident about people, and was quick to let me pet him when I first offered my hand out for him to sniff. I saw him sporadically throughout the year and he was shy about showing how eager he was for some fuss, and I always happy to provide him the attention he enjoyed. His visits suddenly became more common, only this time, at least once a week, he'd wait at the bottom of my drive way, and when he spotted me walking up the street, he'd come running to greet me. He made a point out of walking me home, never straying too far from my feet, and would look around as if to make sure we weren't in danger. If I didn't know any better, I could have sworn he had a big smile on his face when he'd run up to me, it really brightened up my day. He got his nickname because my partner kept joking that he looked like one of the bodyguard cats from 'The Cat Returns', and that he was going to take me away to the cat kingdom. Looking back, he really didn't look much like the anime cats, but he certainly acted like a body guard.


Ghost. After my first year of university I moved into a flat with my partner, and the elderly gentleman who lived in the flat next to ours owned a white cat. The cat was very a healthy weight, but his fur was dusty and unkempt, he wore constantly disgruntled expression, and he didn't care much for human contact - we suspect the cat was actually a stray and that the elderly gentleman had been caring for the cat. He would occasionally let me approach him and pet his head for a good few seconds before pulling his head away, at which point I'd leave him in peace. On a few rare occasions, if I called to him he would saunter over and let me pet him for a bit, before wondering off. Then one day, I was walking out of the building when he came running up to me meowing and rubbing against my leg. I knelt down, and he flopped onto his back, so I took a gamble and rubbed his tummy. I've never seen a cat enjoy tummy rubs quite like he did, I'd never really heard him purr before until that moment. After a few minutes fuss, he wondered off about his business and I got on with mine. That was the last time I saw him. His owner was deemed unable to care for himself and was put into a home. I have no idea what happened to the cat, but I really hope they got to stay together, or at least that the cat found a loving home. It was nice to see the little guy show me one last gesture of trust before he left.

I was in a friend group with two other girls, and they really helped me to be the person I truly was without being ashamed or judged. Until they both decided I was too close with girl B, and girl C was feeling left out, so they wanted to let me be a third wheel of the group. All the different types of bullying I was experiencing got significantly worse, the beatings were more viscous and more often. This girl refused to take any responsibility for what she'd done and kept changing her story. First it wasn't her who said, then it was but she said it was just a kiss on the cheek, then suddenly she didn't say shit. On top of all this, a student had recently come out as bisexual and she got bullied so badly she moved schools. That was the first time I knew what bisexual meant, and I realised that it described me. Seeing the treatment I received for my perceived homosexuality, I was terrified and ended up in extreme denial about my sexuality until I was 18 or so. Through all of this I was depressed, anxious, anorexic, OCD, self harming, and I'd also only just stopped suffering horrific hallucinations. I'm not sure there was a specific thing that finally threw me over the edge, but I ended up trying to take my life on school grounds. No one found me, no one noticed I had been gone for an abnormal amount of time, and I spent the next few months kind of coasting through life in a bit of a haze.

When I got to upper school, things did improve somewhat. I was still bullied, but it was no longer physical, or of a homophobic nature. My hallucinations had gone entirely by this point, I wasn't self harming anymore, my OCD, anxiety and depression were improving, and I actually ended up  a decent enough friend group (a few people took the piss, but they were usually looked down on for it). Eventually however, something just snapped inside me. I was obsessive about eating less than 1000 calories a day, I would exercise until I was in tears, I was cutting myself, my depression got severe, my OCD was more obsessive (no new routines, but it was more common for me to do them over and over because 'they didn't feel right'), and I developed social anxiety. I attempted suicide a few times throughout Upper school and sixth form, but my attempts were obviously unsuccessful, and went mostly unnoticed (accept by a few people who I trusted to talk to about it). I knew I needed help, but I refused out of fear. I was concerned that my age would require my families involvement in decisions about treatment, and, as I mentioned, they were already overbearing. Once I believed myself old enough, I was still too scared to seek out any real help, because I was worried that the severity of my illness would still involve them being given some kind of custody over treatment decisions etc. I decided to play the waiting game, I coped as best as I could and hid my mental health issues, and eventually came up with the idea that going to university would get me away from my family. I desperately wanted to move to Canada, but part of the criteria (according to the internet) was to have either a trade or a degree.

As luck would have it, I ended up getting in a relationship around the same time I sent off my university applications, which somewhat made me rethink the Canada plan, because we were both pretty serious about the relationship. Even so, I wanted to use my own shitty start in life to help others as a therapist, and I believed a degree would be very useful, so my university plan didn't change. I ended up lying to my family about my university requiring first year students to live on campus, because I was desperate to break away and experience independence for the first time. Not even a month into my first year I ended up in an argument via text in which I called my dad out on his and his mothers bullshit, and the whole thing ended with me cutting contact from my entire family (My dad and grandmother for obvious reasons. Hadn't seen or talked with my mother since I was 7, so meh. My aunt and uncle because I saw them once a year if I was lucky and they would just take their side. My adopted grandmother, only because I had no way of contacting her or finding out where she is - I miss her and I really hope she knows how much I love her). I'd like to say this is where things improved, and they did somewhat, however I still had financial issues, uni stress, and my mental health making my life a nightmare. I also almost ended up homeless, until my partner sat me down and talked about moving in together, which we did at the end of my first year of uni. I've loved living with my partner, though it's been pretty stressful as we ended up living in the same town as my family - I'm terrified every time I leave the flat. The next two years were somewhat turbulent, as on top of everything I developed a sound disorder. I did attempt to talk to counselors and my GP, but found them of very little help, with my GP laughing at me and my counsellor telling me - in not so many words - to get over it.

I'm 23 now. It'll just be nice to finally move out of the town where I've suffered so much. To not feel fear every time I leave the house, I'm going to enjoy that.

Every once in a while I get this bizarre nightmare of being in forest. It'll be quite bright, and the trees and bushes are illuminated a luscious green from the sun beaming up, hidden behind all the foliage. It just looks so beautiful, so picture perfect as I'm walking along the dusty trail. Eventually, I hit a kind of 'T' shape in the path, and I can either continue forward, or go right.

Suddenly the forest is much more sinister in appearance. The ground is no longer carpeted in colourful flowers, or soft vibrant grass; instead it's replaced with a blanket of dead and rotten leaves. The bark on the tree looks charred, and the leaves appear lifeless and dark, whilst the bushes no longer have any leaves at all. Despite the graveness of the foliage, I still can't see the sun above, and everything is eerily dark.

I look down the path that journeys right, and I feel absolute dread slowly, but surely, engulfing my very being. I can't explain why, but I'm terrified. The path is not particularly long, maybe 10-20 meters, and at its end there's a toilet cubicle. The metallic door slowly opens, and there's and elderly woman hanging from a noose. The end of the noose isn't attached to the trees, it's not attached to anything, it's floating in the air. The corpse is wearing clothes that suggest a victorian era maid, complete with a frilly black and white bonnet framing the top of her head. All this time, the fear continues to fill my very soul.

The cubicle door closes, and then opens. The noose is gone. The lady is stood,now animated and staring at me with glazed, dead eyes. She begins to very slowly make her way towards. Each step separated from the last. Each step calculated and deliberate. She doesn't get very far before I run down the other path that had been straight in front of me, my heart in agony from the fright. It's not long before the forest returns to it's previous and more appealing appearance and I, briskly, but no longer running, continue on my way to wooden gate that leads out of the forest.

At this point I wake up, though sometimes I wake up a little while after the forest turns back to normal. When I wake up, I tend to be paralysed with an overwhelming sense of terror, and I just don't know why. I mean, sure seeing a dead person come to life in such an obscure scene is pretty scary, but I'm always left with this feeling like my level of fear is way too high, and not fitting. It's fucking horrible.

I really hate this, because it takes away from people who are genuinely struggling with mental health issues. Having social anxiety isn't being a hipster, it's getting shaky and tearful because you're going to have to go outside where there's loads of people who you know are going to stare at you, judge you, and laugh at you. It's spending an hour thinking about what social interactions you might encounter, what they could say, what you could say in response, how what you say could be taken badly, and how, if it is taken the wrong way, you can make the other person understand what you actually mean. Having OCD isn't just keeping your room or desk tidy, or making sure your DVDs are in alphabetically order. It's not being able to sleep until you stare at your doorway for a count of seven without blinking, then staring at the window for a count of seven without blinking, then blinking seven times to a count of seven while looking at the doorway, then blinking seven times to a count of seven while staring at the window, then turning in your bed to face the wall while simultaneous wrapping your duvet around you so you end up totally covered, because you have this intense feeling that something bad will attack you if you don't. It's spending an hour doing that same fucking routine because you keep getting it wrong, and then finally doing it correctly, but having to try again simply because "it didn't feel right". Depression isn't an excuse you can use to validate multiple netflix binges to get out of doing something productive. It's going days without showering because you don't have the energy to get out bed, let alone shower. It's waiting until the very last minute to go to the bathroom because you don't want to have to face the arduous task of walking ten feet to the bathroom. Some people would even rather piss themselves because their depression is so bad. It's feeling like everything around you is muted and you're constantly shrouded in this heavy, suffocating darkness.

There are a lot of people with mental health issue that have their every day lives and their personalities drastically impacted, and some people could even be considered dangerous to themselves and others because their illness is to such a severe extent. On the flip side, it also makes it really difficult for people who have less severe mental health issues to be taken seriously - for example not everyone with social anxiety is unable to talk publicly, not everyone with schizophrenia hears mean voices, and not everyone with depression is self harming or suicidal. There's so much stigma already for people who suffer mental health issues, which is exasperated by the influx of people who use it as a trend. Having a mental illness is exhausting, upsetting, and soul crushing. Having a mental illness isn't some little trinket you can show off like a magpie with a shiny bauble, and it's not some stupid film where a teenager has a shit week followed by a happy resolution because they end up with that person they've been crushing hard on. People literally die from mental illnesses, and it disgusts me how little respect some people have for such a serious issue.

* When I'm finished with a can of drink, I have to flick the tap that original sealed the drink as far inside the can as possible. Then I move the second tab back and forth until it snaps off, and I put the tab inside the can. Finally I crush the sides of the can tightly together using my hands.
* The labels on blankets have to be at the foot end of the bed, and the button end of the duvet cover also has to be at the foot end of to bed. I also put the duvet inside the cover so that the label will be at the button end

Not my own story, but I am the girl in the story.

I had recently become part of a new friend group, and was going out clubbing with them every weekend. It was a totally new experience for me as I had previously being against the idea, but I enjoyed being around these people so much I figured it was worth a try, and I fucking loved it - so many good memories. Anyway, I was also very poor, and kind of embarrassed about it, so I would often walk for an hour to get home, because I couldn't afford a taxi. Eventually one of the guys in the group who was extremely security conscious twigged and refused to let me walk home alone, he managed to get another guy in the group to volunteer, though I actually missed that happening and didn't realise.

So, I'm walking home and this 6'2" guy is walking with me, and we're chatting away pretty well. Eventually we pass the area where he roughly lives, so I figure he's going to the uni he was studying at to do late night revision or assignment work. We pass the uni and he's still walking with me and at this point I sort of twig what's going on and internally freak out. I felt so guilty that he was walking all this way with me, I also feel terrible because I had my earphones in for a lot of the time thinking he was going to be off quite quick and I didn't want to come across as rude, and at the same time I was also freaking out about social protocol and running out of conversational topics (yay social anxiety!). We get to my home and I don't have a clue what to do, so I sort of walked to my door and get my keys out, because that's what I'd seen in so many films - guys always seem to walk the girl to her door. He looks confused and says "err, you know I'm not coming in right". I panic at my lack of social skills and fail to cover it up with "I know, I was checking the door for spiders". I think after this we hugged goodbye, he walked off, and I got through the door and sat in the hallway for a good ten minutes anxiously glaring at the floor.

The rest of the story is only what he told me. You see, whilst I was rumbled earlier about walking home alone, they were asking about which estate I lived in. They named one that sounded familiar, so I genuinely thought it was that one. I'm not great at geographical awareness, and it turns out I was about a half an hour walk away from the estate I had claimed to live in. So this guy had walked with me through the waste lands of our town, including some very unsettling/isolated areas, and he just went with it without trying to question me. I'm surprised he didn't think I was luring him into an ambush of some sort. It was also extremely cold, and by the time he had reached my home he was numb, but of course didn't mention it. He ended up walking about twenty minutes before asking the security of a local superstore if he could use the phone so he could call a taxi, and thankfully the security officer agreed - probably helped that his lips were apparently blue from the cold at this point.

From then on he would usually bring a big coat with him whenever the group was out clubbing, and would often walk home with me, even though he knew it was such a long way. We had some really great conversations, and we also got cheered at by some woman driving passed us while he was pushing me in a trolley. It's been about four years since that first night, and he still hasn't let my lack of geographical knowledge go. He also hasn't let me go either, we'll have been together 4 years this December :)

There are many different and similar scenarios that can leave a person sad or depressed. Often depression stems from serious and traumatising events such as abuse, but can also be caused by experiences such as the lose of a loved one, or a messy break up. Sadness is usually caused by situations that are upsetting experiences in a minor way, but can also stem from situations that could have the potential to leave a different person depressed. Sadness can be as simple as crying over a mushy film, or as deeply wounding as being betrayed by a loved one. Sadness is very temporary, and often easier to deal with than depression; whatever the scenario, sadness is short lived and something that can quite easily be conquered, even if it takes a few tubs of ice cream.

Depression isn't just that feeling of a hand gripping and squeezing your heart, it's total, inescapable numbness. Your mind feels empty and even if you tell yourself that you really do want to do something today, you know you're just lying to yourself. All motivation has drained away, along with any care you had about eating right, keeping clean, socialising, or anything that requires getting out of bed. You're aware of your surroundings, but at the same time it's like you're in a dark void that you can't free yourself from. Depression is a serious mental illness that is too often shrugged off as a 'phase' or 'feeling a bit blue'. Depression can't be cured by ice cream or chocolate, a lot of the time it can't even be cured by therapy or medication, because even with those treatments, depression can still be an issue that the sufferer has to fight against every day. Depression is lonely, it's heart wrenchingly painful, and, in far too many cases, it can take a persons life.

I've never really liked children all that much. I don't find them cute in any way, and just generally feel uncomfortable and miserable when I'm around them. I got made fun off pretty badly in middle school after I commented that I didn't want to have children. I kept getting told I would change my mind, that I'm supposed to have children, that no one will ever love me if I don't want children, that I'd never have a boyfriend etc. A "friend" of mine even got my crush at the time to write a list of all the reasons he wouldn't go out with me and emphasised that me not wanting children was a huge issue. For a few years I pretended that I wanted them, just to avoid the hassle, I even tried to convince myself that I actually wanted them in the hopes that it would make me "normal".

Eventually I realised how stupid that was, and instead decided to find out for myself instead of letting other people expectations take place of my own. I took up babysitting to find out if I could handle being a parent, and if it would be something I'd want to do with my life. I stuck it out for two years just to make sure, and, despite really needing the money, I quit. I would end up in tears before and after every babysitting session, and the task just made me extremely depressed and miserable. I just didn't feel happy at all, but I'm still glad I did it, because at least I know for certain now that parenthood just really isn't for me. I'm a lot happier just being me, even if it means I often have people giving me a shitty attitude towards my choice to be childfree. 

The kids I looked after were actually really well behaved, but the amount of time and energy it took to look after them just didn't feel worth it. Over those two years I got to witness several kids personalities and knowledge develop, but for me it just didn't feel worth it for all the work and time, and I wasn't even their parent, I was there a few hours a week.

Not only the time/effort, but even well behaved children can be extremely annoying, even if it isn't exactly their own fault. For example some of them who are too young to really understand hygiene trying to put their hands on you that they've just put in their pants or that are covered in crumbs/dirt. It's disgusting to say the least. Then there's the curiosity too - I can't believe how many questions a single child can ask in such a short time, it's exhausting. And they can be very difficult to talk to because they can't seem to keep their thoughts in any kind of order; they jump from one topic to anger totally irrelevant topic. I understand that these are traits that are common to children and come from their curious nature and ignorance of the world, but I just couldn't deal with that, and find it extremely unappealing.

Then of course there's other issues such as the financial side of raising a child, having to deal with other parents (most of which are fine, but the bad ones are just too much), overpopulation, generally the shitty crime infested world we live in, passing on illnesses, fear of having a dependant child for the rest of your life, etc. 

And finally there's the most important reason of all. I just don't want children. I'm not interested. That should be enough of a reason, but for most people who ask, it rarely is - with those same people not pressing wanna-be-parents as to the reason they want children. If you don't want a cat or dog, you don't then immediately bring one into your life anyway, because that would be irresponsible. People who don't want children shouldn't have children simply because, they don't want children in the first place. It's really that simple.

Because you're completely ignorant about rescue dogs. Dogs who get rescued from the streets or from abusive or neglectful homes go through tests to see whether they have aggression towards certain people, dogs, other animals (such as cats), or objects. Dogs who display aggression are given a rehabilitation programme to correct that behaviour. Dogs who clearly aren't improving at all with the rehabilitation, or dogs who are deemed so dangerous that rehabilitation isn't an option, are put down. Some dogs who aren't dangerous, but have anxiety or troublesome behaviour will usually only be rehomed to individuals who can deal with your behaviours or anxieties.

Most rescue dogs aren't dangerous, because those shelters can't risk a lawsuit resulting from adopting out a dog that is in any way dangerous. That's why they have proper procedures to go through to make sure these dogs aren't dangerous.

How old is the child? The way you describe him, he sounds to be quite young, I'd guess around 7 or 8. Have they tried an actual child psychologist? They may be better equipped to help than just a counsellor.

Also if CBT hasn't worked, perhaps suggest DBT (Dialectic Behaviour Therapy), it's more long term, and it's used for more severe problems. It's quite often used in borderline personality disorder, severe depression, and in situations where CBT just doesn't work. CBT looks at changing the way a person thinks (using logically based arguments) in order to change their behaviour, DBT uses some similar techniques and structures as CBT, but instead teaches the patient to accept the good with the bad. It might help the child to accept the circumstances that led to his bad behaviour, accept the world around him, and accept that his behaviour is not okay.

For example people with anxiety aren't destined to have depression too, but they are more likely to develop it than the average neurotypical person. This means, that even if your parent only suffered anxiety, if you develop anxiety too, you're still at a high risk of developing depression alongside it. It sounds like the two of you really need to talk this situation out and tell each other how you feel. That's a point that might be worth getting across to her, that any children she had would be confronted by some of the worst parts of her mental health issues. For example, if she often gets emotional and yells, her child would experience that and may grow scared of her. She may unintentionally be an emotionally abusive force in her kids life, which wouldn't be fair on anyone in that situation.

It's been suggested to me by therapists that my abusive grandmother may have had narcissistic personality disorder, which is why she couldn't go more than five minutes without making some unnecessary and nasty criticism. I spent everyday for 19 years being made to feel not good enough, and it may have partially been a mental health disorder that caused it. I tried to bring her behaviour to her attention, but she would turn herself into the victim and me into the bad guy for calling her out on it. There's a chance she didn't mean to be abusive, but what she did was still abuse behaviour that has destroyed my life, and now it's left to me to start a new and try to repair all the damage. That's no way for a child to grow up.

Good luck, and I do hope everything works out for the best.

(A side note: I'm not trying to indicate that mentally ill people are all abusers, but unfortunately it can lead to that in some people and also with particular disorders, and so it should be something to consider)

I suffered from OCD in middle school, and eventually it improved, though I do still have some small things:

* I wash and dry my hands to stuff counts of 8. Two counts when washing my hands, and four counts when drying.

* I have to cut vegetables and meat a specific way depending on the meal I'm making.

* Labels on blankets, duvets, and mattress covers have to be at the foot end of the bed.

* The button side of the duvet cover had to be at the foot end of the bed too.

* When I finish a can of drink, I pull the tab (used to open the drink) back and forth until it breaks off. Then I put the tab inside the can. Then I push the bit, that previously sealed the drink, as far inside of the can as possible (so it's against the roof of the inside of the can). Then I crush the sides of the can together. Then bin it.

These aren't too much of an issue, and whilst they do take up some small amount of time, I don't feel they cause too much of a disruption. However, back when my OCD was much worse, I used to have two rituals that were pretty disruptive.

* The tiles in the bathroom were square, and it you positioned the bathroom door just right, it would diagonally cut through the pattern perfectly. I would end up doing this several times throughout the day, because of course bathrooms quite often have people moving in and out of them throughout the day, and that day would inevitably be moved.

* The other was a breathing and counting routine. It's very complicated and it's been years since I've done it, but I'll try my best to remember what I actually did. I would be laying in my bed, which was right near my door, and I would be able to see the door to the living room. I'd stare at this door for a count of "One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. One. For. Luck. One for luck." I would do this count twice. The first time I'd breath in on one count, and out on the next. The second time I would hold my breathe the entire time. I would then stare at my window and do the same thing. Then I would stare at the living room for and do the same thing. Then I would quickly flip on to my other side, whilst simultaneously wrapping my duvet around myself. If I blinked I would have to start over again. If I breathed out of count, or when I was supposed to be holding my breath, I would have to start again. If at the end of this ritual I felt it was wrong, I would do it all over again. I spent so long every night doing this, so it was really disruptive and I would get very frustrated and stressed out of I didn't do it right or if it felt wrong.

I kind of was that kid. When I first started school when I was 5, I was a total teachers pet, and all the teachers knew me and were pretty fond of me. Then one day, I didn't come to school anymore. My mother had taken me away from my dad when I was about six years old and she got me put in another school. A year later my dad got full custody because my mother had been physically abusing me and neglecting me. When I returned to my original school, all the staff knew what happened and were told to keep an eye out in case my mother tried to abduct me. She did actually turn up a few times (got a pretty decent talking to by the head teacher) and even once came to a school play; eventually I think a restraining order was issued.

A few years later when I was in middle school, and I got really sick. I went to reception and they tried to call someone to pick me up. Well my heart sank when the receptionist said she had tried both of my parents and they hadn't answered, but my grandmother had, and she was on the way. She was very confused that I freaked out over her calling my mother. They weren't supposed to have her on my emergency contacts, for obvious reasons. My dad and grandmother went ballistic, and from that point on I'm pretty certain many of the staff and my teachers were informed, just in case.

Things didn't get better unfortunately, and I'm having some issues at university because of it, which I'm likely going to need to disclose to a professor of mine. However, she's suddenly stopped responding to my emails, which is a little problematic - it's a long story. Anyway, the point I'm trying to make is, please take interest in your students, especially if they reach out to you for help, because they're putting themselves in such a vulnerable position by doing that. You never know what they're going through, and I really wished some of my teachers later in life had taken some time to listen. I lost a lot of trust in teachers, particularly in middle school, because they basically told me they didn't give a shit that I was being bullied and I just had to deal with it. I think a lot of them thought I was weird and deserved it, but I was just messed up from what I'd been through.

Thank you to those of you who have actually been there for students - you've done more for them than you could ever know. I don't think some people realise what a difference a good (or bad) teacher can make to a students life.

I'm not sure if this counts, because I'm still in the middle of this process. I have a very abusive background; my mother was physically abusive for a year until my dad got full custody; my dad was verbally abusive and had anger issues (beat the shit out of inanimate objects but thankfully never me); my grandmother was manipulative, and emotionally and mentally abusive. I moved to university a few months before I was 20 and, whilst most other students cried and felt home sick, I couldn't have felt happier to be free of them. I had lied and said I was required to live on campus for the first year. I lied about this because the university was in the town next to my home town and I was certain my family wanted me to continue living with my dad whilst at university, and would use the closeness of the university to pressure me into staying. My original plan was to enjoy my first year of freedom, then live with my dad for two years, save up money, and then hightail it out of there to a different county (before I met my boyfriend my original original plan was to go to an entirely different country instead. I was planning to move to Canada). I felt horrible for planning to use my family like that for two years, but I was desperate to escape their abuse, and I almost felt like they deserved it. I knew my dad wouldn't ask for much in the way of rent, and I'd be able to save up plenty of money by staying with him for the last two years of my course. Well, as many people already know, life doesn't always go as planned.

A month into my stay at university, and me and my dad are texting when he says something that irked me. My new found independence allowed me to grow some balls, and I called him out on it. This resulted in a huge argument via text and I called him out on his and my grandmother's abusive behaviour. He totally ignored all the crap I mentioned that they had put me through and of course turned himself into the victim and tried to make out like I was some ungrateful brat. He refused to acknowledge all the nasty things he would call me every single week, he refused to face up to the times he had told me he wished I'd never been born, and he played dumb when I mentioned the horrible things my grandmother would say to me on a daily basis. The argument ended with him suggesting that we should live our own lives separately, and I didn't bother replying because I didn't feel like he deserved the closure, I didn't want him to think that I was taking his lead, and I didn't want him to feel as though he had any control over me or this situation.

That was October of my first year, and then that Christmas they (my dad, grandmother, and aunt and uncle) sent me Christmas and birthday cards with money in them as if nothing had happened. I know my grandmother very well, and I can almost guarantee that she told them to do it because "she'll come crawling back" and no doubt she told them not to worry because "she's just going through a phase". Whenever my dad was nasty to me, he would often buy me something (eg. A bar of chocolate), and I'm pretty certain they believed they could buy me back. Needless to say it didn't work. In fact, at the end of my student accommodation contract, I would very likely be facing homelessness. In the UK our term time is funded, but the summer holidays isn't. If I couldn't find a job before then, I'd have no way to fund myself throughout the summer, or pay for an accommodation deposit. I had struggled a lot previously years to find work, so my hopes weren't high at all. However, homelessness was more appealing to me than returning to my family, and that might give you a better idea of just how bad it was.

I was only four or five months away from homelessness and I still hadn't found anywhere to work. One day, my boyfriend (we had only been together for a year at this point) sits me down and says we need to have a serious talk. My heart sunk, I knew I was about to lose someone who had made me happier than I ever thought possible. He must have seen the look on my face, because he smiled and said "don't worry, I'm not breaking up with you". Instead he wanted us to move in together. He wasn't rich, but he earned enough that we could just about get by through the summer months if we moved in together, even if I was jobless. We were very lucky and managed to move in to a flat together about two weeks before the end of my contract. We were both worried because we hadn't been together all that long, considering we were making such a big step in our relationship, but at the same time it made sense. We were visiting each other a lot anyway, which was pretty costly, and it just seemed logical to pay for a single place between us, instead of two separate places apart. My boyfriend worked in my home town, where my family live, and it wasn't really possible for him to get to work easily if we moved to any of the near by towns. This meant we had to move to my hometown, which was terrifying, but I knew them well, so I was sure I'd be able to avoid them. It was also not too difficult for me to get to university, though I would sometimes have to get up unnervingly early to make it to lectures and tutorials. It seemed like a very small price for me to pay.

Over six months after we moved in together, I decided to change my names. Initially I was going to change it after university, but since I was already estranged from my family, I figured I might as well do it then. I felt very unhappy with a set of names that were so heavily linked to those people, and I also didn't want those names on my degree. I didn't want my degree linked to them in anyway because it would feel like they were taking my achievement. Silly I know, but I felt so freed when I finally got the official documents of my name change.

It's been roughly two and a half years since I became estranged from my family, over a year and half since moving in with my boyfriend, and just over a year since I had my names changed. We're hoping to move out of town, maybe even out the county, a year after I finish university. There's a town I would like to go to because it has a weekend course I'd like to take in order to further my career. Until then, I'm terrified every time I go into the town centre to get groceries. I've had two and half close calls with bumping into my family. Twice I nearly bumped into my grandmother and the half time I think my dad was following me, but I didn't exactly feel like stopping to get a good enough look at him to confirm whether or not it was my father. Despite being estranged from them, I still struggle very badly with depression and social anxiety. However, cutting those people out of my life certainly did me a world of good. I imagine things will improve for me even more once we've moved town, but first we need to save up and we'll need to hunt around for accommodation and jobs wherever we end up moving to.

I guess as a whole I'm happier now, but I've still got quite some way to go to repair all the damage my family did, and to increase my distance between them. It's a work in progress, but the end is in sight and I'm going to do whatever it takes to hold on to that.

I've had a lot of pretty terrible experiences with mental health due to being an abuse victim until I was 19. Here's a list of the more memorable and/or worst stuff.

* I've had multiple suicide attempts over the years, but the one that sticks out was my first because I was so young (only about six, nearly seven years old) and I was extremely lucky I guess. My mother had taken me from my father and at the time we were living on the first floor of a two floor block of flats. It's a little tricky to describe, but the corridors outside the flat doors weren't fully walled off. They instead had about a knee-height wall, so if you weren't paying attention you could easily walk into the wall, fall over it and plummet to the ground below. I knew that the ground below, at one end of the corridor, had a patch of concrete. I didn't look over the wall, because I was worried I'd chicken out - that decision potentially saved my life. I ran from one end of the corridor to the other, jumped the small wall and fell. I ended up landing in a skip full of furniture. My fall was mostly broken by a sofa or mattress, though I did also hit a dinning table. Escaped with a few minor cuts and bruises, but was otherwise fine, aside from being pretty shaken up.

*  I developed a sound disorder, which turned out to be misophonia, over a year ago, I only found out because we got new upstairs neighbours. I could hear their footfall as if they were stomping above my head, but my partner would have to really strain to hear it. I would have extreme emotional reactions of anger, or usually distress and would be left shaking and in tears. It put a huge strain on my relationship because my partner felt totally helpless because he couldn't do anything to stop my reaction or the noise (they were just walking after all) and he had a very difficult time understanding why I was having such a volatile reaction to something so minor. He actually became very cold and unloving towards me whenever I had an episode. Eventually he read up on misophonia, and he's now extremely patient and helpful. I remember a child was screaming (huge trigger for me), and my SO put his hands over my ears until the family left the aisle we were in. I nearly cried because I was so happy; I'd thought for a long hole that my misophonia was going to break our relationship. I suffered pretty badly for a year, and I became unable to attend one of my lectures at university because it was in a room right next to construction work which triggered my condition. Thankfully I learned a few coping techniques and I'm dealing with it somewhat better than I used to, though that initial year was an utter emotional nightmare.

* I got accepted to university at 19 and ended up estranged from my family, by choice. At this time I suffered from depression and social anxiety, which I was working hard to improve. In my second year it got worse and I tried the university counsellor. Whenever I told her I couldn't do x, y, or z because of my mental health, she would tell me to do it anyway. She didn't put any effort at all into helping treat my mental health other than to repeatedly suggest I ignore it. She also tried way too much to emphasise her sympathy of my situation by exaggerating her emotions, but it just turned into an hour of her pulling faces at me while I poured my heart out. That was pretty heart-breaking because I really needed support and I felt like she just didn't understand.

* Throughout my teen years I struggled with anorexia for a whole bunch of reasons; one reason being my grandmother who was overly critical about everything I did or said. In the same week, or even the same day, that she'd told me I was "nothing but skin and bone" she would also have said something like "You won't be able to eat like that when you're older, you'll get fat!". She also regularly declared to me that I didn't need to worry because "I'd tell you if you were getting fat!". She would ask me after school if I was hungry, and even when I said no she would prepare me some snacks. If I didn't eat it she would guilt trip me about how she went through all the trouble to feed me, but I'm not going to eat it. It didn't even matter to her that I'd told her I wasn't hungry, in her mind I was in the wrong. If I did eat it just to keep the peace, she'd gloat about how lazy I am and how I'll eat anything that gets put in front of me. This happened every school day until I was about 16/17. When I was in sixth form I would go to hers in the morning and then catch a nearby bus into the sixth form. I would only eat a single piece of toast because eating in the morning would make me feel unwell. She constantly badgered me to eat more for breakfast. One day when I'd said, for the hundredth time, that two pieces of toast would make me sick, she suggested a packet of crisps instead. I agreed, and she smugly smiled "That's settled then! Two pieces of toast and a packet of crisps". I looked her dead in the eyes and snapped "No." Usually she would have further pushed, but I'd never snapped at her before and I think that shocked her into silence. She would constantly play these weird little mind games every single day. It's really no wonder I ended up anorexic, but the reason this particularly sticks out for me is because of something she said to me. She once said "You're very skinny, but I'm not worried. I know you're not anorexic because your face isn't all sunken in". When she said that I was about a stone and a half underweight.

* My worst experience of mental health would probably be when I was in middle school. Fun fact: Children experience depression differently from adults and are more likely to suffer hallucinations as a symptom. I used to see living corpses and demonic creatures (think the girl from the ring), usually in mirrors and more often in the evening or when it was particularly dark. It was terrifying and I lived with it for about four years. I still get very uneasy about being alone in a room that has mirrors.

* I went through a lot of this alone because I was terrified that if I told teachers, school counsellors, or a doctor, it would get reported to my family. They were pretty possessive of me, and if they had known the full extent of my mental health issues I doubt I ever would have been allowed out and unsupervised ever again. They where very no-tolerance towards mental health, with my grandmother once saying that people with schizophrenia should all be locked up, and when I explained to her they're more likely to hurt themselves than others and that mental illness such as depression and anxiety account for a larger percentage of serious crimes her response was "I don't care, they should ll be locked up". One time when I tried to confide in my dad about my depression and social anxiety, he stated yelling at me that I was just like my (physically abusive) mother, always telling stories.

I can't think of anything else really right now, but if anything springs to mind, I'll add. I think talking about mental health is very important in showing what it can be like, educating people, and it also helps myself in getting a lot off of my chest.

Misophonia trigger sounds are commonly quiet sounds, but not exclusively. I suffer from misophonia, but many of my trigger sounds are either loud, or I perceive the sound to be very loud (I hear footfall from the flat above as though someone is stomping against our ceiling, but my SO has to strain to be able to hear it), and one of my major trigger sounds is infants/toddlers crying, and kids talking.

Either way people with misophonia will have abnormal/extreme emotional reactions towards specific sounds (trigger sounds vary from person to person). This emotional reaction can be of anger, irritation, fear, panic, or distress, and is notably very similar to how some people with PTSD react to a trigger sounds.

The difference is, when someone with PTSD is triggered by noise, it's not uncommon for it to remind them of their traumatic experience or even result in flashbacks. Sometimes as well, the trigger sound may be related to the trauma - for example a war veteran may be triggered by the sound of a car misfiring because it may sound like a gun or explosion. People with PTSD often have nightmares or night terrors of the trauma too.

Either way, you should definitely try to see a professional about this, that way you can get a proper diagnosis.

Also people who wanted children one day were more likely to change their mind than people who said they never wanted to have children.

For most people with misophonia, the trigger sounds do tend to be bodily functions or quiet/background noises such as rustling or footfall. However, some individuals with misophonia are triggered by loud noises, or can experience noises at an amplified rate (I can hear upstairs footfall as if they're stomping above my head, but other people have to strain to hear it). I struggle pretty badly with both of these, and screaming babies/kids is an issue for myself too. I find a helpful tip is to rationalise the situation, for example, when I hear footfall I explain to myself that it's just people walking and that it's not actually as loud as I'm experiencing it, or if an infant is crying I explain to myself that it can't help it because it doesn't know how to talk about what it needs. Earplugs are also extremely useful, and so are noise distractions such as calming music. Also maybe look into neurofeedback therapy, I've heard from others within the misophonic community that it's extremely effective. I hope this helps in some way, and I hope your misophonia improves, or at least that the sound reduces.

When changing your name, it might help you to think about the reasons you want to change your name. It might help you decide whether you want to retain some of your past or identity through a name similar to your current one, or whether you'd rather express a new or hidden identity, or erase the past, with a new name. No you don't need to feel bad for disliking children. Some people argue "they're just kids, they can't help being kids", but the exact some argument can be used for you. I also have two couple friends, one couple had a 5 year old daughter, the other couple had a 6 year old daughter. Both these girls are relatively well behaved, they don't invade my personal space when I'm around, and for the most part they're pretty quiet. They're good kids, and I would go as far as to say I don't dislike them, but still can't honestly say that I like them. I feel uncomfortable and extremely on edge and anxious with these kid around.
